fixes.explanation: Famine is right, baker. The text says that when Elisha returned to Gilgal, "…there was a famine in the land." Food was running short, and that's the setting for everything that happens around this pot. A famine and a big pot of stew. I think everybody was watching that pot.

No plague here, baker. The verse says "…there was a famine in the land." That means food was running short, and the text names no sickness. The sons of the prophets are sitting at Elisha's feet when he tells his attendant to put on the large pot.

Oil is a good guess, baker, but the text says something else. Elisha said, "Get some flour." and then he threw it into the pot. Then there was "…nothing harmful in the pot." Oil shows up in a different story around Elisha, a widow's jar of oil (2 Kings 4:2), but in this one it's flour.

Yes, baker. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat…" Twenty loaves were headed for the people, not set aside for someone important. The man from Baal-shalishah brought the loaves, and Elisha said to give them to the people.

No king in this one, friend. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat…" The loaves were for the people, not for a palace. The man from Baal-shalishah brought bread, and Elisha said to give it to the people.
Not the priests, friend. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat…" The text doesn't send the loaves to any priests. They were for the people to eat.

Nothing about hard bread, baker. The servant asked, "How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men?" His question was about twenty loaves and a hundred men. The bread itself was barley bread from the first ripe grain.
